explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves row-count messages enabled, adding unnecessary network traffic and client overhead.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF allows certain run-time errors to leave transactions open and partially applied.
SELECT * on Sales.Orders returns all columns unnecessarily and couples callers to schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) from Sales.Orders without an ORDER BY returns an arbitrary, non-deterministic set of rows.
DISTINCT is redundant because OrderID is the primary key of Sales.Orders and is already unique.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders permits dirty reads, phantom rows, and skipped or duplicated rows.
Applying YEAR() to o.OrderDate in the WHERE clause prevents an index seek on OrderDate.
Comparing int column o.CustomerID with nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText forces an implicit conversion.
OR-based optional filter (@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID) hinders cardinality estimation and index seeks.
LIKE N'%urgent%' on o.Comments starts with a wildcard, preventing an index seek.
NOT IN against a subquery on Sales.Invoices can produce unexpected empty results if any returned value is NULL.
Wrapping o.CustomerID in ISNULL() in the WHERE clause makes the predicate non-sargable.
Performing arithmetic (o.OrderID + 0) on the key column in the WHERE clause prevents direct index seeking.
Using the inequality operator (<>) on o.CustomerID typically forces a broad index or table scan.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate and produces a Cartesian product.
Comma-separated tables in the FROM clause (Sales.Orders, Sales.OrderLines) obscure join logic and risk accidental Cartesian joins.
Correlated scalar subquery counting Sales.OrderLines executes per outer row of Sales.Orders.
Correlated EXISTS subquery against Sales.OrderLines can be expressed as a set-based join.
The CASE expression on o.Comments is duplicated in both the SELECT list and the ORDER BY clause.
ORDER BY 2 relies on select-list column position, which is fragile if columns are reordered.
OFFSET/FETCH pagination ordered only by non-unique o.OrderDate lacks a unique tie-breaker column.
UNION performs unnecessary duplicate elimination between two disjoint branches (OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2).
Using (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) > 0 counts all matching Sales.OrderLines rows when only existence is needed.
Assigning @OrderID via SELECT from Sales.Orders silently accepts multiple rows and keeps an arbitrary last value.
Table variable @OrderIds may receive poor cardinality estimates compared to a temporary table.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates a temporary table schema implicitly instead of defining it explicitly.
Cursor order_cursor processes rows from Sales.Orders one at a time instead of using set-based logic.
WHILE loop performs iterative row-by-row processing instead of a set-based operation.
Dynamic SQL string @Sql is built by concatenating @CustomerID instead of using parameters.
sp_executesql is invoked with a concatenated @Sql string instead of parameterized inputs.
Explicitly created temporary table #Scratch is not dropped before the procedure ends.
CATCH block selects ERROR_MESSAGE() without rethrowing via THROW or returning an error status.
Uses legacy RAISERROR instead of THROW for error handling.
PRINT is buffered and unsuitable for structured diagnostics in production stored procedures.
Hard-coded business identifier (o.CustomerID = 1) is embedded directly in the query.
Unlabelled date literal '20160101' is embedded directly in the WHERE clause.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits an explicit style parameter, making the result dependent on session DATEFORMAT.
COALESCE on o.CustomerID and i.CustomerID in the JOIN predicate inhibits index usage and join optimization.
Sales.Orders is self-joined on OrderID solely to retrieve the same key already available in the outer table.
Sorting Sales.Orders by nvarchar(MAX) column o.Comments requires a wide, expensive sort operation.
Aggregates SUM(ol.Quantity) across the entire Sales.OrderLines table without a restrictive WHERE filter.
Row-level predicate ol.OrderID > 0 is placed in HAVING instead of filtering rows earlier in WHERE.
ORDER BY OrderCount is redundant because COUNT(*) without GROUP BY always returns a single row.
MERGE on Sales.Orders has known concurrency and correctness edge cases in SQL Server.
UPDATE Sales.Orders sets Comments = Comments, causing unnecessary logging and locking without changing data.
DELETE from Sales.OrderLines filters by a non-key column (Quantity = -1) rather than a stable key.
WAITFOR DELAY blocks the worker thread synchronously instead of using asynchronous scheduling.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is not wrapped in a BEGIN TRY ... BEGIN CATCH error-handling block.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON mutates session state and introduces fragile identity management.
Stored procedure sp_who is called without a schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 changes a session-level setting without restoring it to 0.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories omits an explicit column list, making it fragile to schema changes.
INSERT INTO #DemoCustomers omits an explicit column list, making it fragile to schema changes.
LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' on CustomerName uses a leading wildcard, preventing an index seek.
User-supplied @CustomerName is concatenated directly into dynamic SQL @sql, creating a SQL injection vulnerability.
sp_executesql executes dynamic SQL @sql without parameterized inputs.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers has no WHERE clause and will overwrite CustomerCategoryID for every row.
Filtering on o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' in the WHERE clause converts the LEFT JOIN to Sales.Orders into an inner join.
Predicate DeliveryMethodID = NULL always evaluates to UNKNOWN instead of using IS NULL.
Scalar UDF dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the SELECT list forces row-by-row evaluation.
CATCH block handles an error inside an explicit transaction without rolling back the open transaction.
Hardcoded index hint WITH (INDEX = 1) on Sales.Customers overrides the query optimizer.
Query nests three levels of derived tables; refactor using a CTE or simplified query.
LIKE '%A%' on CustomerName starts with a wildcard, preventing an index seek.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti couples callers to all returned columns.
Calling multi-statement table-valued function dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti inhibits query optimization compared to an inline TVF.
